Project finance & ESIA · South Africa

Dated land baselines for EAPs, lenders and project teams

Structure registers, land-cover baselines and the imagery history of a site, delivered as layers your team can put in its own maps and reports, and dated evidence of what changed between site visits. For environmental assessment practitioners, engineering consultancies, lenders’ advisers and the project teams they work for. We work as your supplier, and a person reviews every result.

Tell us about your project footprint Discuss a subcontract

The problem, in your words

Baselines needed early, sites seen rarely

“We need a structure count before fieldwork starts.”

Sizing a social survey, a census or a specialist study starts with knowing how many structures stand in the footprint and where. A count from the air lets you plan the fieldwork on facts.

“When did the clearing start?”

An environmental control officer’s audit, a rectification application or a dispute can turn on roughly when ground was cleared or a structure went up. Dated imagery is often the only record.

“We can’t visit as often as the monitoring plan says.”

Lenders’ advisers and monitoring teams visit on a schedule, and much happens in between. Dated comparisons show where the next visit should go.

“What was on this land before financial close?”

Before investment or acquisition, the land’s history and the current structures on it belong in the due-diligence file.

Who this is for

  • Environmental assessment practitioners
  • Engineering and E&S consultancies
  • Environmental control officers
  • Lenders’ environmental and social advisers
  • Resettlement and land-acquisition teams
  • Developers’ environmental managers
  • Due-diligence and transaction teams

Baselines for EAPs and consultancies

Layers for your own maps and reports

Environmental authorisation in South Africa runs under the National Environmental Management Act and the EIA Regulations 2014 (GN R.982, GG 38282), as amended in 2017, 2018, 2020 and 2021, and registration with EAPASA has been required of environmental assessment practitioners since 8 August 2022. The practitioner owns the assessment; what we supply is the land data it needs, early and dated.

For a project footprint, corridor or study area, we deliver a structure layer with reviewer categories, estimated households with the assumptions stated, settlement growth trends around the site, a land-use and land-cover baseline, a comparison of alternative sites or alignments, and slope, drainage and flood screening. Where your team has flown its own drone survey, we run the analysis on those orthophotos. Everything arrives as GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ or Shapefile for your GIS team, with a PDF report where you want one.

Some projects arrive with less environmental process than others: compliant power lines inside the strategic transmission corridors are excluded from environmental authorisation under the power-line standard (GN 2313), so the land baseline for them is needed from another source.

What you receive

  • A structure layer with reviewer categories
  • Estimated households, with the assumptions stated
  • Settlement growth trends around the site
  • A land-use and land-cover baseline map
  • A comparison of site or route alternatives
  • Slope, drainage and flood screening
  • GIS layers for your own maps, and a PDF report where scoped

Environmental authorisation

Roughly when, and roughly where

For audits, rectification and applications, we compare dated imagery of the site against the footprint in the authorisation:

  • Clearing and construction footprints compared between dates, from satellite scenes and drone surveys.
  • Roughly when clearing or construction happened, from the imagery history of the site.
  • Structures and activity inside the no-go buffers or sensitive areas you define.
  • A pre-development land-cover baseline, and the progress of rehabilitation afterwards.

What it shows, and what it doesn’t

Imagery shows what was visible on the ground on each capture date. It supports an audit, an application or a response to a directive; it does not by itself prove compliance or non-compliance, and it does not replace the environmental control officer’s inspection.

Between site visits

Dated evidence for lenders’ advisers and monitoring teams

Construction and earthworks

Construction footprints and earthworks compared between dates, including drone orthophotos of resettlement sites and work fronts, subject to the approvals and security clearances each job requires.

New structures in the footprint

New and removed structures inside the footprint and its buffers, flagged automatically and confirmed by a reviewer, with before-and-after views.

Clearing and revegetation

Clearing outside approved areas and revegetation of rehabilitated ground, compared between dates from Copernicus Sentinel data.

Dated very-high-resolution archive scenes, a new capture where the archive is too old, or imagery the project already holds can all feed the comparison. Capture dates depend on satellite availability and weather and are never guaranteed. Remote evidence complements site visits; it never replaces them.

Lender-financed projects

Resettlement cut-off-date records

IFC Performance Standard 5 applies to projects financed by DFIs and Equator Principles banks, including transmission lines and independent power projects. South Africa has no single national resettlement regulation, so a project’s resettlement plan combines national law with the lender’s standard.

We produce a dated record of the structures in the project footprint around the cut-off date, with imagery, coordinates, IDs and reviewer categories, and re-survey the footprint afterwards so that structures built after the cut-off date are flagged and confirmed. The record supports your census and asset inventory and the IFC Performance Standard 5 cut-off-date records; it does not replace the census, set the cut-off date or determine eligibility.

In the standard’s own terms

IFC’s guidance ties the cut-off date to the completion of the census and asset inventory. A dated structure register, made from imagery captured close to that date, gives the census team and later grievance reviews a fixed reference.

Resettlement cut-off-date baselines

Before investment or acquisition

Land due diligence

Before financial close or an acquisition, we assemble the imagery history of the site, route or portfolio, a land-cover baseline, and the current structures on its rights of way, in its concession or inside its hazard zones. The history says what was built, cleared or changed, and roughly when; how much archive exists varies by place. It is not a title, tenure or valuation check.

Imagery history and land due diligence

How it works

From footprint file to layers in your report

  1. Scope

    You send the footprint, corridor or study area, the dates the record must reflect and how the layers will be used. We agree the method, imagery and deliverables in a written proposal.

  2. Build the baseline

    Structures, land cover and the imagery history are mapped from dated satellite scenes, open datasets and any imagery the project holds.

  3. Compare between visits

    Re-surveys on the schedule you set show new structures, clearing and construction, confirmed by a reviewer.

  4. Deliver to your team

    GIS layers and reports go to the contacts you name, with every imagery source stated, and its date where the source gives one.

Honest scope

What we do, and what we don’t

What we do

  • Supply dated structure, land-cover and change layers to your team
  • Show roughly when clearing or construction happened, where imagery exists
  • Support census, asset-inventory and cut-off-date records
  • Work as a supplier to your consultancy, in your formats

What we don’t do

  • Carry out the environmental assessment or sign off its conclusions
  • Stand in for the census, the ECO’s inspection or the lender’s reviewer
  • Set cut-off dates or decide eligibility and compensation
  • Promise a capture date for any imagery

Frequently asked questions

Can you work as a subcontractor to our EAP or engineering team?

Yes. We supply structure counts, land-use and land-cover baselines, imagery histories and GIS layers for your own maps and reports, and answer to your project manager. The assessment, its methods and its conclusions stay yours.

Can your baseline stand in for the census and asset inventory?

No. It is a dated record of the structures in the footprint, with imagery, coordinates and IDs, that supports your census and asset inventory under IFC Performance Standard 5. Field teams still carry out the census and asset inventory, and compensation needs ground verification.

Does the imagery set the cut-off date?

No. The cut-off date comes from your resettlement process, and IFC guidance ties it to the completion of the census and asset inventory. Our record documents what was on the ground on the imagery dates around it.

Can you show when clearing outside the authorised footprint started?

Roughly, where dated imagery exists. We compare scenes before and after the date that matters and report the first one in which the clearing is visible and the last in which it was not. That supports an audit or an application; it does not by itself prove compliance or non-compliance.

Can the record be used in a dispute?

It is a dated, credited record that supports legal and community processes. If it is to be used as evidence about unlawful conduct in South Africa, check POPIA’s prior-authorisation rule (s57) with counsel first. See POPIA and aerial imagery.

Does remote evidence replace site visits?

No. It gives you dated evidence between visits and helps you plan where the next visit is needed. Capture dates depend on satellite availability and weather, so they are never guaranteed.

Tell us about your project footprint

The footprint, corridor or site polygons (Shapefile, GeoPackage, KML or GeoJSON), the dates the record must reflect and how the layers will be used. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
